Maneuver

/muh-NOO-ver/ — rhymes with mover · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To maneuver is to move or steer something with skill and careful control through a tight or tricky space.

With one quick maneuver, the pilot slipped the plane between the storm cells.

Worked Example

The surgeon worked carefully through the narrow space, maneuvering the delicate instrument to extract the stone without damaging the surrounding tissue.

Maneuver precisely describes skillful movement in a constrained, difficult space. Plain words like 'move' fail to capture the expertise, careful control, and tight-space navigation required. Maneuver is exact because it emphasizes both the skill involved and the challenging conditions that make the action noteworthy.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

move: to change place in any way

shift: to move slightly to a new spot

steer: to guide a vehicle's direction

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

careen: to swerve wildly, out of control

flounder: to move clumsily and helplessly

Where it sits · how much skill the steering takes — move → position → maneuver → navigate

move vs. maneuver: 'Move' covers any change of place at all, but to maneuver is to move with skill through a tight or tricky space.

position vs. maneuver: To position something is to set it in place, while to maneuver is to steer it there past obstacles.

navigate vs. maneuver: To navigate is to plot and follow an entire route, going a step beyond a single skillful maneuver.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — man(u)

Root — man(u): hand (Latin)

Root — -euver

Root — -euver: to work (from Latin operari, reshaped through French) (Latin (via French))

Put it together

Put it together: Man(u)- means 'hand' and -euver comes from Latin operari, 'to work,' reshaped by French. To maneuver is literally 'to work by hand' — careful, hands-on handling of something tricky.

Use the root in a new word: manuscript

Use the root in a new word: manuscript: The author mailed her handwritten manuscript to three different publishers.

Word Choice

neutral / formal

Maneuver is the right word when you are describing skilled, careful movement in a constrained or difficult space. It emphasizes both the expertise required and the tight conditions. For simple movement, use 'move.' For directing a vehicle in open space, 'steer' works. But when you need to convey skilled navigation through tight spaces or tricky situations, maneuver is more precise.
